Question: I spend most of my time on work only I can do as a leader, not on tasks my team could handle.
I hold back from jumping in to fix problems myself when a team member could solve them.
I measure my success by what my team achieves, not by my own individual output.
I set aside regular time for planning, coaching and thinking ahead, not just day-to-day work.
I am comfortable letting go of work I used to be the expert in.
What work are you still doing yourself that you should be directing others to do? What keeps you holding on to it?
I delegate the whole outcome, not just the steps, and let the person decide how to get there.
When I delegate, I am clear about the result, the deadline and how much authority the person has.
I match what I delegate to each person's strengths and development needs.
Once I delegate something, I avoid taking it back or redoing it myself.
My team members take ownership and bring me solutions, not just problems.
Think of a task you delegated recently. What went well, and what would you do differently?
I know my top three priorities, and they guide how I spend my week.
I confidently say "no" or "not now" to requests that do not fit our priorities.
When new work comes in, I discuss trade-offs instead of simply adding it to the list.
I protect my team from unnecessary work and constantly shifting demands.
I can explain to stakeholders why something is or is not a priority without feeling guilty.
Which requests or demands make it hardest for you to say "no" or "not now"? Why?
My team understands how their work connects to the goals of the wider organization.
I explain the "why" behind decisions and priorities, not just the "what".
I set clear expectations about quality, deadlines and what good looks like.
I check that people have understood my direction before they start.
My direction stays consistent, so my team is not confused by changing instructions.
Where does your team most often get unclear about direction? What do you notice when it happens?
I follow up on commitments at the agreed time, without needing reminders.
I hold people accountable consistently and fairly, including high performers.
I address missed commitments early and directly, rather than letting them slide.
Meetings I lead end with clear owners and next steps.
I keep the commitments I make to my team and stakeholders.
What gets in the way of follow-through for you or your team? What would help most?
